entries.test: Public demonstrations and documented production use would show whether AI could independently perform a Hollywood writer's or writers' room's work as of August 2023.
entries.note: The Hollywood context fixes the relevant meaning of writer. The present-tense assertion can be extracted separately from the forecast.

entries.test: Dated demonstrations and documented production use establishing when AI could realistically perform a Hollywood writer's or writers' room's work would test the predicted continuing inability.
entries.note: “For some time” supplies no definite deadline. “Nor do I believe” expresses his prediction here rather than merely a possibility.
“Soulless” is an aesthetic judgment without an agreed factual test.

entries.test: Contemporaneous model evaluations, hallucination studies, and documented corporate adoption decisions would test recurring errors, deteriorating performance, and adoption despite demonstrated unsuitability.
entries.note: This bundles several assertions. Its factual core concerns model reliability and corporate adoption practices.
The predicted time penalty is explicitly qualified by “likely.”

entries.test: Public employer statements and changes to job classifications or skill requirements would show whether theoretical AI capability is used to justify treating more labor as unskilled despite output-quality problems.
entries.note: “Even if” allows poor output as a possibility; “even though” asserts it. The normalization also drops the stated rationale of theoretical computer capability.

entries.test: Publicly documented replacements of artists, writers, and other workers with AI, accompanied by company statements about automation, would test the predicted readiness to replace those roles.
entries.note: “Gladly” and “in a heartbeat” emphasize readiness; the central prediction concerns observable replacement decisions.

entries.test: Documented corporate AI deployments that accept reduced output quality for projected cost savings would establish the asserted willingness.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion supplies the AI context. Willingness can be demonstrated through actual decisions and public statements.

entries.test: Corporate AI spending data and public incident investigations would show whether an investment surge with inadequate safeguards produced several automation failures causing losses smaller than Knight Capital's $440 million loss.
entries.note: The comparison supplies a concrete class of costly automation failures. No deadline is stated.

entries.test: Public staffing announcements and documented workload changes would show whether employers use AI to eliminate entire roles or substantially increase workers' assignments without requiring demonstrated task competence.
entries.note: “Regardless of capability” removes a qualification rather than introducing a conditional antecedent.

entries.test: Public incident reports and company responses would establish whether excessive reliance on AI caused a company a sequence of conspicuous failures, such as harmful advice, erroneous marketing, or costly operational mistakes.
entries.note: The examples give “deeply embarrassing” a sufficiently concrete reading. The examples themselves are possibilities, not separate firm predictions.

entries.test: Public company experiments, service changes, and financial results would show businesses testing reductions in human involvement and customer service to identify the point at which those reductions cause losses.
entries.note: “Human workers” narrows “the human element,” which also includes human interaction and service. The source predicts testing the limits, not necessarily continuing every experiment until losses occur.
